articles.title: A mysterious 4,000-year-old wall is rewriting North Africa’s history
articles.summary: A remarkable 4,000-year-old defensive structure discovered in Morocco is rewriting what scientists thought they knew about ancient North African civilizations. The massive fortifications reveal unexpectedly sophisticated prehistoric societies and suggest that the region played a much greater role in Mediterranean history than previously recognized.
articles.content:
In the hills of north-west Morocco, overlooking the river that gives the site its name, research at Oued Beht is bringing to light a previously unknown chapter of the region’s past. The discovery of a substantial built structure suggests that, during the second millennium BC, communities in north-west Africa were actively shaping their environment. They were also engaging in broader networks of interaction across the Mediterranean world.

Previous research by the Oued Beht Archaeological Project had already brought to light what is likely the earliest and largest agricultural complex ever discovered in Africa outside the Nile Valley. It dates to around 5,400 to 4,900 years ago. New excavations carried out in 2023 – in which we took part – have now deepened our understanding of the site.

Our new study shows how we uncovered the earliest known large-scale construction of a probably defensive nature in north Africa beyond the Nile Valley. It’s about 4,000 to 3,500 years old.

It’s not known exactly what threats these wall-like structures were designed to counter. They likely relate to increasing competition over land, resources, and possibly control of movement through the landscape, rather than to “invaders”. Constructions like these suggest communities felt the need to protect themselves or assert power over strategic locations.

This discovery pushes back the evidence for organized defensive architecture in the Maghreb and suggests that societies in this region at this time were more complex and structured than previously believed.

Our study also reveals how the ridge of Oued Beht would become a focal point again in the medieval period, during the 11th to 13th centuries AD. The same defensive structure was rebuilt, a hamlet or farm was established on a nearby hilltop, and people were buried in a cemetery between the two areas.

Together these findings provide rare archaeological insights into rural communities during both prehistoric and medieval times. They help us understand how societies developed and maintained themselves in a region too often left out of the history books.

A prehistoric hub in the Maghreb

For a long time, the later prehistory of north Africa’s Maghreb region (the Mediterranean countries of Morocco, Algeria, and Tunisia) has been poorly understood. Compared with neighboring areas such as Iberia in south-western Europe or Athens in the eastern Mediterranean, archaeological evidence was often fragmentary. In the last few years this has changed completely.

Excavations at Oued Beht have revealed a large concentration of human activity spread across at least ten hectares. The earliest major phase dates to the mid-fourth and early third millennia BC, or the Final Neolithic period.

Environmental evidence from plant and animal remains in the prehistoric era indicates a farming community cultivating crops such as barley and wheat. They also exploited wild plants and kept livestock.

The site was also an important center of craft production. Thousands of polished stone axes and other tools have been discovered, along with finely made pottery, sometimes decorated with painted patterns.

It’s still uncertain whether prehistoric Oued Beht functioned as a permanent village, a seasonal center, or something less familiar. But it was clearly a major focus in the landscape of north-west Morocco.

The defensive wall

The presence of potentially ancient earthworks and walls had been noted since the 1930s. The French archaeologist Armand Ruhlmann first documented a configuration of three walls, with the fourth side protected by the natural scarp of the ridge, describing a defensive éperon barré (barred spur). Their precise nature and date remained uncertain until now.

New excavations have clarified the existence of a multi-phase ditch, rampart and wall built across a narrow section of the Oued Beht ridge between the river and a ravine. This cut off and protected the ridge’s southern tip.

Radiocarbon dating of deposits associated with these structures gave us the timelines in our study.

They place its original construction at a time equivalent to the Bronze Age of the remaining western Mediterranean. This makes it the earliest confirmed defensive construction in north Africa outside Egypt.

What was this construction for?

This structure raises important questions about the society that built it. Building an embankment and ditch system required planning, coordination and the mobilization of labor. This suggests a community capable of organizing complex construction initiatives.

During the earlier Neolithic phase, activity at Oued Beht focused on the larger and more open northern area of the site. By the period of our new study, focus had shifted to the narrower, more defensible southern ridge. This may reflect a shift in settlement strategies.

Mediterranean connections

The second millennium BC was a dynamic period across the Mediterranean. In southern Iberia, Argaric societies (about 2200-1550 BC) in today’s Europe were developing complex, often hilltop settlements. They were characterized by planned architecture, advanced metallurgy (especially bronze production), and marked social hierarchies visible in burial practices. These communities often constructed fortified sites, and strategically located settlements controlling surrounding territories.

Increasing evidence suggests that communities in north-west Africa were connected to wider Mediterranean networks. This includes today’s Spain and Portugal. The discoveries at Oued Beht indicate that the Maghreb was not isolated. It participated in broader processes shaping the western Mediterranean.

The defensive system at the site may reflect wider transformations in social organization and regional interaction. There may have been growing competition over resources, control of movement, and more formalized leadership structures.

Rewriting history

The discoveries at Oued Beht highlight how much remains to be learned about the deep history of north Africa. The defensive wall shows that communities here were able to coordinate large construction projects and points to social transformations that are only very tentatively beginning to be recognized.

The medieval remains demonstrate that the ridge was used again many centuries after the prehistoric settlement had been abandoned. Oued Beht was not simply a single-period settlement but a landscape repeatedly selected by different communities across millennia.

As research continues, this location may become key to understanding how societies in the Maghreb evolved from early farming communities to the medieval rural world.
articles.reasoning: The discovery of a 4,000-year-old defensive wall in Morocco provides significant new insights into the complexity and sophistication of ancient North African societies, rewriting historical understanding of the region's role in Mediterranean history. This archaeological breakthrough has broad cultural and historical significance, revealing organized social structures and Mediterranean connections in prehistoric times, and thus has a positive real-world impact on knowledge about human history and heritage.
articles.personality_title: Ancient 4,000-year-old wall in Morocco reveals new history of North Africa
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – In north-west Morocco, an archaeological site called Oued Beht has been studied for years. It is known for early farming remains and tools, but until recently, little was known about large constructions there.

**What happened** – In 2023, researchers discovered a 4,000-year-old defensive wall at Oued Beht. This wall includes ditches and ramparts built across a ridge, showing complex construction. Radiocarbon dating confirmed it was made during the Bronze Age, making it the oldest known defensive structure outside Egypt in North Africa.

**Impact** – This find changes what scientists thought about ancient North African communities. It shows they were organized, able to plan large projects, and connected to Mediterranean cultures like those in Spain and Portugal. It also suggests these societies faced competition over land and resources, leading them to build defenses.

**What's next step** – Researchers will continue excavating to learn more about how these communities lived and interacted. The site also has medieval remains, showing it was important for thousands of years. Future studies might reveal how early farming villages grew into medieval rural societies in the Maghreb region.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The discovery of a 4,000-year-old wall in Morocco reveals that ancient North African societies were more advanced and connected than previously known, reshaping our understanding of the region’s history.
articles.personality_title_fr: Un mur vieux de 4 000 ans au Maroc révèle une nouvelle histoire de l’Afrique du Nord
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Dans le nord-ouest du Maroc, un site archéologique appelé Oued Beht est étudié depuis des années. Il est connu pour ses traces précoces d’agriculture et d’outils, mais jusqu’à récemment, on connaissait peu de constructions importantes sur place.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – En 2023, des chercheurs ont découvert un mur défensif vieux de 4 000 ans à Oued Beht. Ce mur comprend des fossés et des remblais construits sur une crête, montrant une construction complexe. La datation au radiocarbone a confirmé qu’il date de l’âge du Bronze, faisant de lui la plus ancienne structure défensive connue en Afrique du Nord en dehors de l’Égypte.

**Impact** – Cette découverte change la vision des scientifiques sur les communautés anciennes d’Afrique du Nord. Elle montre qu’elles étaient organisées, capables de planifier de grands projets, et connectées aux cultures méditerranéennes comme celles d’Espagne et du Portugal. Elle suggère aussi que ces sociétés faisaient face à une compétition pour les terres et ressources, ce qui les a poussées à construire des défenses.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs continueront les fouilles pour mieux comprendre la vie et les échanges de ces communautés. Le site possède aussi des vestiges médiévaux, montrant son importance pendant des milliers d’années. Les futures études pourraient révéler comment les premiers villages agricoles ont évolué en sociétés rurales médiévales dans la région du Maghreb.

**Phrase clé** – La découverte d’un mur vieux de 4 000 ans au Maroc révèle que les sociétés anciennes d’Afrique du Nord étaient plus avancées et connectées que ce que l’on pensait, transformant notre compréhension de l’histoire de la région.
articles.personality_title_es: Un muro de 4.000 años en Marruecos revela nueva historia del norte de África
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – En el noroeste de Marruecos, un sitio arqueológico llamado Oued Beht ha sido estudiado durante años. Es conocido por restos tempranos de agricultura y herramientas, pero hasta hace poco se sabía poco sobre construcciones grandes en el lugar.

**Qué pasó** – En 2023, investigadores descubrieron un muro defensivo de 4.000 años en Oued Beht. Este muro incluye zanjas y terraplenes construidos en una cresta, mostrando una construcción compleja. La datación por radiocarbono confirmó que fue construido durante la Edad de Bronce, siendo la estructura defensiva más antigua conocida en el norte de África fuera de Egipto.

**Impacto** – Este hallazgo cambia lo que los científicos pensaban sobre las comunidades antiguas del norte de África. Muestra que estaban organizadas, podían planear grandes proyectos y estaban conectadas con culturas mediterráneas como las de España y Portugal. También sugiere que estas sociedades enfrentaban competencia por tierras y recursos, lo que las llevó a construir defensas.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores seguirán excavando para aprender más sobre cómo vivían e interactuaban estas comunidades. El sitio también tiene restos medievales, mostrando su importancia durante miles de años. Estudios futuros podrían revelar cómo las primeras aldeas agrícolas se convirtieron en sociedades rurales medievales en la región del Magreb.

**Frase clave** – El descubrimiento de un muro de 4.000 años en Marruecos muestra que las sociedades antiguas del norte de África eran más avanzadas y conectadas de lo que se creía, cambiando nuestra comprensión de la historia de la región.
articles.image_prompt: A warm, detailed painting of an ancient, sturdy earthen wall and ditch winding along a rugged ridge overlooking a calm river in northwest Morocco, with symbolic clusters of polished stone tools and painted pottery resting nearby, under a soft natural palette of earth tones and muted greens, evoking a sense of early complex communities shaping their landscape and connecting across the Mediterranean.

articles.title: Samarkand: A ‘living museum’ on the Silk Road grapples with a tourism boom
articles.summary: As the sun sets over Samarkand’s majestic Registan, its last rays glint across the turquoise mosaics. Dusk settles on the ancient square where great trade routes have crossed for centuries.
articles.content:
Tourists linger at the stalls as the lights come on, lending the square an air of mystery.

The Registan is part of historic Samarkand, a UNESCO World Heritage site. But this is more than a city of monuments. People live here; schools, shops and workshops are open, and old neighbourhoods stand alongside new districts.

UN News visited ahead of World Cities Day to ask: how can civil leaders preserve its heritage while it keeps growing?

That question is at the heart of Samarkand’s “Silk Road” International University of Tourism and Cultural Heritage, which trains specialists in both fields from a campus in the city centre.

The university’s rector, Professor Muhsinjon Kholmukhamedov, told UN News that for centuries Samarkand was a crossroads not only for trade, but for ideas, crafts and cultures, flourishing in the eighth and ninth centuries and again in the Timurid era, when it became a centre of science, culture and the arts.

UN News

A first for UN Tourism

The university began working with the World Tourism Organization, now UN Tourism, in 2023 and renewed the partnership this year.

“We are the first partner university of this organization. We have established cooperation in several areas,” the rector said.

It is translating courses from the organization’s online academy for residents and preparing to open an INSTO tourism observatory – the first in Central Asia.

The observatory will track not only visitor numbers, but tourism’s impact on jobs, the urban environment and residents’ daily lives, as similar observatories already do from Barcelona and Vienna to Gifu in Japan and Nuevo León in Mexico.

Undoing the repairs of the past

Heritage preservation is another strand of its UN work, through a UNESCO Chair. One challenge, Mr. Kholmukhamedov said, is the legacy of restoration work in the 1990s.

“Unfortunately, gypsum, concrete and rebar were used then. We are now conducting research with experts and providing evidence-based recommendations on the use of modern composite materials that do not damage the historic fabric of the monuments,” he said.

Laser scanning lets researchers build three dimensional models of buildings and spot dangerous deformations in time. “If there is a critical tilt, we try to support the structure,” the rector said.

He calls Samarkand a living museum, where people go to work, meet friends and eat out beside monuments of global significance – a city that teaches its residents to value history.

Visitors feel that energy too. “Visiting Samarkand always reminds me of its special hospitality and energy. It is truly inspiring to see the city grow so vibrant and culturally rich,” UN Resident Coordinator in Uzbekistan Sabine Machl told UN News.

UN News

Why Timur chose Samarkand

Legend has it that Amir Timur picked his capital by having meat hung in several cities to see where it would take longest to spoil.

In Samarkand, the rector said, it stayed fresh longest – thanks, he believes, to the climate, the Zarafshan River and the nearby mountains.

Legend or not, Samarkand’s place in a fertile oasis at the crossroads of trade routes shaped its fortunes – and made it a welcome stop for merchants after arduous journeys.

A crossroads once more

Today, according to the rector, new railways are expected to connect Uzbekistan with China and Afghanistan, and on to South Asia, while a planned high speed highway should cut the Samarkand–Tashkent journey to about two and a half hours. Both are due for completion between 2030 and 2032.

The skies are busier too, with direct flights from Samarkand to more than 40 destinations.

UN News

A tenfold tourism boom

According to Mr. Kholmukhamedov, about 1.2 million tourists visited Uzbekistan in 2016, compared with nearly 12 million in 2025. He estimates Samarkand alone received around seven million visitors last year; more than 10 million came in the first nine months of 2026, and the city expects around 14 million by year’s end.

Many come for the food – not least Samarkand palov - a rice pilaf – cooked and served in layers with local sesame oil. Uzbek palov culture is on UNESCO’s Intangible Cultural Heritage list.

UN News

Homes for the people

Rapid growth is raising urgent questions about housing for Samarkand’s own residents – fitting, as this year’s World Cities Day theme is Urban Renewal: Affordable Housing for All.

More than 1,100 apartment buildings have gone up in Samarkand Region over the past eight years. UN-Habitat is now developing the Samarkand Housing Profile, Uzbekistan’s first, with the national Government.

Our generation’s task is to preserve Samarkand while making it future proof so that it stays liveable for future generations while keeping its identity, through resilient communities — Katja Schaefer

The city’s master plan to 2040 foresees a big expansion of housing, but also looks at the condition, energy efficiency, affordability and upkeep of existing homes – most of them individual houses. The Profile will recommend ways to make adequate housing more affordable, resilient and sustainable for all.

“In Samarkand, heritage is not only the monuments. It is also the mahallas, the traditional neighbourhoods where people live and where community life happens.

“The best approach is to upgrade homes and services in place rather than replace them: better water, heating and energy efficiency, sensitive renovation that respects the historic urban fabric, and new growth steered to areas outside the historic core,” Katja Schaefer, a UN-Habitat representative working on the project with local specialists, told UN News.

“Above all, residents should be involved in decisions about their neighbourhoods. Done this way, heritage and better living conditions support each other,” she said.

“Every era has left its mark,” she added. Much of the Soviet era housing and infrastructure is now outdated, and since independence the city has grown rapidly, at times without a plan, squeezing the green spaces that make it pleasant to live in.

UN News

Growing a ‘green city’

Ms. Schaefer hopes the new master plan and the Green City Action Plan will tackle these challenges together.

In August, Samarkand and Tashkent joined the Green Cities Network of the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), a group of cities working towards greener, healthier urban environments.

“What struck me most in Samarkand is how much of its greatness came from being a meeting place. Its position on the Silk Road made it a crossroads of trade and cultures for centuries, and it drew scholars from across the region.

“Under Ulugh Beg, it became one of the world’s leading centres of astronomy, mathematics and science. That spirit of exchange and innovation is still part of the city’s identity,” she said.

“Our generation’s task is to preserve Samarkand while making it future proof so that it stays liveable for future generations while keeping its identity, through resilient communities,” Ms. Schaefer said.

articles.personality_title: Samarkand balances heritage and growth amid booming tourism
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Samarkand is an ancient city in Uzbekistan, famous as a key stop on the historic Silk Road trade route. It is recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage site, known for its beautiful monuments and rich cultural history. Recently, the city has seen a huge increase in tourists, raising questions about how to protect its heritage while supporting growth.

**What happened** – Samarkand’s “Silk Road” International University of Tourism and Cultural Heritage is working with UN organizations to study and manage tourism’s effects. The city expects about 14 million visitors in 2026, a big rise from 1.2 million in 2016. Alongside tourism, local leaders are planning new housing projects to help residents and improving conservation methods to protect historic buildings. They use modern technology like laser scanning to monitor and maintain ancient structures.

**Impact** – This approach is unique because it combines preserving ancient monuments with caring for the people who live there. Instead of replacing old neighborhoods, the city plans to improve homes and services while respecting history. The partnership with UN groups also brings expertise and global examples to help Samarkand grow sustainably. This balance helps keep the city both a living community and a world-famous heritage site.

**What’s next step** – Samarkand will continue expanding housing with a focus on energy efficiency and affordability. New transport links like railways and highways will connect the city more closely to other regions. The planned tourism observatory will track how visitors affect the city’s jobs and environment. Samarkand is also joining green city networks to improve sustainability and quality of life for residents.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Samarkand shows how a historic city can welcome millions of visitors while carefully protecting its culture and supporting its community through smart planning and international collaboration.
articles.personality_title_fr: Samarkand allie patrimoine et développement face à l’essor du tourisme
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Samarkand est une ville ancienne d’Ouzbékistan, célèbre pour être un arrêt clé sur la route historique de la soie. Elle est classée au patrimoine mondial de l’UNESCO, reconnue pour ses magnifiques monuments et sa riche histoire culturelle. Récemment, la ville a connu une forte augmentation du nombre de touristes, ce qui soulève des questions sur la manière de protéger son patrimoine tout en soutenant sa croissance.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – L’Université internationale du tourisme et du patrimoine culturel de la « Route de la soie » à Samarkand collabore avec des organisations de l’ONU pour étudier et gérer les effets du tourisme. La ville attend environ 14 millions de visiteurs en 2026, contre 1,2 million en 2016. Parallèlement au tourisme, les responsables locaux prévoient de nouveaux projets de logements pour aider les habitants et améliorent les méthodes de conservation pour protéger les bâtiments historiques. Ils utilisent des technologies modernes, comme le laser, pour surveiller et entretenir les structures anciennes.

**Impact** – Cette approche est unique car elle combine la préservation des monuments anciens avec le soin apporté aux habitants. Au lieu de remplacer les vieux quartiers, la ville prévoit d’améliorer les logements et les services tout en respectant l’histoire. Le partenariat avec les groupes de l’ONU apporte aussi expertise et exemples mondiaux pour aider Samarkand à grandir de manière durable. Cet équilibre permet de garder la ville à la fois vivante et site du patrimoine mondial.

**Prochaine étape** – Samarkand continuera d’étendre ses logements en mettant l’accent sur l’efficacité énergétique et l’accessibilité. De nouvelles liaisons de transport comme des chemins de fer et des autoroutes rapprocheront la ville des autres régions. L’observatoire du tourisme prévu suivra l’impact des visiteurs sur l’emploi et l’environnement. Samarkand rejoint aussi des réseaux de villes vertes pour améliorer la durabilité et la qualité de vie des habitants.

**Message en une phrase** – Samarkand montre comment une ville historique peut accueillir des millions de visiteurs tout en protégeant soigneusement sa culture et en soutenant sa communauté grâce à une planification intelligente et une collaboration internationale.
articles.personality_title_es: Samarcanda equilibra patrimonio y crecimiento ante el auge del turismo
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Samarcanda es una ciudad antigua en Uzbekistán, conocida por ser una parada clave en la histórica ruta de la seda. Está reconocida como Patrimonio Mundial de la UNESCO, famosa por sus hermosos monumentos y rica historia cultural. Recientemente, la ciudad ha visto un gran aumento de turistas, lo que genera preguntas sobre cómo proteger su patrimonio mientras crece.

**Qué pasó** – La Universidad Internacional de Turismo y Patrimonio Cultural de la «Ruta de la Seda» en Samarcanda trabaja con organizaciones de la ONU para estudiar y manejar los efectos del turismo. Se esperan alrededor de 14 millones de visitantes en 2026, un gran aumento desde 1,2 millones en 2016. Junto con el turismo, los líderes locales planean nuevos proyectos de vivienda para ayudar a los residentes y mejoran métodos de conservación para proteger los edificios históricos. Usan tecnología moderna como escaneo láser para monitorear y mantener las estructuras antiguas.

**Impacto** – Este enfoque es único porque combina la preservación de monumentos antiguos con el cuidado de las personas que viven allí. En vez de reemplazar vecindarios viejos, la ciudad planea mejorar hogares y servicios respetando la historia. La colaboración con grupos de la ONU también aporta experiencia y ejemplos globales para ayudar a Samarcanda a crecer de forma sostenible. Este equilibrio mantiene la ciudad como comunidad viva y sitio de patrimonio mundial.

**Próximo paso** – Samarcanda seguirá ampliando la vivienda con foco en eficiencia energética y accesibilidad. Nuevas conexiones de transporte como ferrocarriles y autopistas unirán mejor la ciudad con otras regiones. El observatorio de turismo planeado medirá cómo los visitantes afectan al empleo y al medio ambiente. Samarcanda también se une a redes de ciudades verdes para mejorar la sostenibilidad y la calidad de vida.

**Resumen en una frase** – Samarcanda muestra cómo una ciudad histórica puede recibir millones de visitantes mientras protege con cuidado su cultura y apoya a su comunidad mediante planificación inteligente y colaboración internacional.
